text: The rule that a secret never belongs hardcoded into source code doesn't relax just because the code in question is a pipeline definition instead of a script. A pipeline that logs into Azure or AWS to run a provisioning script still needs a real credential — it just can never sit in plain text inside a YAML file tracked by Git.

Writing AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET: "a8f3-REAL-SECRET-9f21" straight into the pipeline file means anyone who can read that file now, or read its Git history later, can read the secret. The exposure is exactly the same as hardcoding a password into application code, just wearing a YAML extension instead.

Both major platforms give you a dedicated store instead. GitHub Actions secrets live under a repository's settings, never visible again once saved, and get injected as an environment variable only while a job runs. Azure DevOps variable groups hold values marked secret, shown with a lock icon. A variable group can even link directly to Azure Key Vault, so the pipeline platform never stores its own copy — it pulls the live value from Key Vault each run.

Referenced correctly, AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET: ${{ secrets.AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET }} puts nothing sensitive into the file at all. That expression resolves to the real value only at run time, by the platform itself, so the YAML stays safe to commit, read, and review by anyone on the team.

Storing a secret correctly solves only half the problem — it can still leak into a build log if a step prints it. Platforms mask recognized secret values automatically, but that protection isn't guaranteed once a value is transformed or embedded in a longer string, so the masking can miss it entirely.

The habit that actually holds up: never echo, print, or log a secret value for any reason, including debugging — check that it's non-empty if you must, but never print what it contains. Next up: a complete, real GitHub Actions pipeline that puts source control, hosted runners, and a stored secret together to run an actual provisioning script.
